description: Solo participant working on Field Shift. I'm a high school student interested in data science and industrial engineering, and I'm building a crop rotation decision-support tool with NASA Earth observation data. Not recruiting for this one.
summary: Crop Shift helps farmers in Türkiye's Konya Closed Basin pick crop rotations that use less groundwater while keeping as much income as possible. The basin uses about 2 billion m³ more water a year than it can supply, NASA GRACE shows its groundwater falling by 3.4 cm a year, and AFAD has mapped 739 sinkholes there. Our app takes 25 years of NASA POWER weather and soil-wetness data for a farm's location, works out how much irrigation each crop needed in every one of those years, and searches all 626 agronomically allowed 4-year rotations for the plan with the highest income under a water limit the farmer sets. It shows four strategies side by side (current practice, best income within the limit, water saver, soil builder) and explains the reasons, evidence, information gaps and risks of each. On the central Konya plain, a 30% water cut keeps about 80% of farm income.
details:
Konya is Türkiye's grain store and its largest sugar beet producer, and most of its irrigation water is pumped from aquifers that are running down. Farmers are told to save water, but they have no easy way to see what a smaller water allowance would cost them or which crops to grow instead. Crop Shift is a free web app built for that decision.

How it works. For any point in the basin the app reads monthly NASA POWER data for 2001-2025: air temperature (mean, max, min), humidity, wind, solar radiation, corrected precipitation and root-zone soil wetness. From these it computes FAO-56 Penman-Monteith reference evapotranspiration, then runs a monthly soil-water balance for eight crop options (irrigated and rainfed wheat, rainfed barley and chickpea, irrigated sugar beet, maize, sunflower and dry bean). Irrigated crops get the water they lack; rainfed crops lose yield in dry years through the FAO-33 yield response. The app then lists every 4-year rotation that passes basic rules (sugar beet, chickpea, bean and sunflower at most once in four years, no legume after a legume, limits on wheat after wheat) and applies pre-crop effects such as a yield bonus for wheat after a legume. A mixed-integer optimizer splits the farm across at most two or three rotations to maximise net income under the water limit, a sugar beet contract cap and soil-health limits. A dry-year switch plans against the driest 20% of the 25 years instead of the average.

What the farmer sees. Four strategies with income, water use, dry-year income, legume share and months of bare soil, each with a plain explanation of why it was suggested, what it gains, what we do not know and what to check locally. A water-versus-income curve shows where cutting water is cheap and where it starts to hurt. Other tabs show the NASA climate trends for the location (on the central plain rain is falling by about 38 mm per decade and temperature rising by 0.6 °C per decade), each crop's irrigation need year by year, and a month-by-month field calendar that shows bare-soil periods, which matter for wind erosion around Karapınar. Prices, yields and costs are editable, because every farm is different.

Checks and limits. Modelled sugar beet water use on the Konya plain (960-1,181 mm per season) falls inside the 1,002-1,177 mm measured in a Konya field trial, though another trial measured less, so our water figures may run high. NASA POWER cells are about 50 km wide, the model runs at a monthly step, and farm costs are 2026 estimates. The tool supports decisions; local agronomists and farmers still make them.

Tools. Python, Streamlit, pandas, NumPy, SciPy (HiGHS solver) and Plotly. Code: https://github.com/berkaydiin/crop-shift

Use of AI. We used Claude (Anthropic) to help with background research, to write and test the Python code, and to draft the documentation and presentation text. We chose the challenge, region and approach, reviewed the outputs and checked key numbers against their sources. AI-assisted code files carry a note in their header. No AI-generated images, video or audio are used.

Next steps. Field-scale water use from Landsat and ECOSTRESS, daily rain from GPM IMERG, a Turkish interface, and tests with Konya farmers and cooperatives.
